name: Well-being therapy (WBT)
evidenceLevel: Developed by Giovanni Fava. In a small trial, well-being therapy reduced residual symptoms after successful treatment of mood and anxiety disorders more than symptom-focused CBT (Fava et al., 1998). In recurrent depression, a sequence of CBT for residual symptoms, lifestyle change and well-being therapy lowered relapse compared with clinical management, with benefits over six years (Fava et al., 1998; 2004). Trials are few and mostly from the developer's group.
purpose: A short structured therapy, often about 8 sessions, usually given after symptoms have improved with medication or CBT, to reduce residual symptoms and protect against relapse. It uses a structured diary of well-being episodes to find the thoughts and behaviors that cut those episodes short, and builds six dimensions of psychological well-being: environmental mastery, personal growth, purpose in life, autonomy, self-acceptance and positive relations with others.
steps: Early sessions: the client keeps a diary of episodes of well-being, however brief, rating their intensity and describing the situation.

Middle sessions: identify thoughts and behaviors that interrupt well-being episodes (for example, 'I don't deserve this' or 'it won't last'), work on them with cognitive techniques, and schedule activities that bring mastery or pleasure.
Final sessions: review the diary against the six well-being dimensions, find areas that are thin or overdone, and set graded tasks to build balance.
Use it after symptoms have improved, as part of relapse prevention, and coordinate with medication plans; any taper decision belongs to the prescriber.
Track residual symptoms with an agreed measure.
script: Instead of tracking only what goes wrong, this week let's track moments when you felt even a little bit well.
What happened that cut that good moment short? What went through your mind?
Looking at your week, which areas feel strong, like your relationships or sense of purpose, and which feel thin?
What's one small thing you could do this week to build on that?
contraindications: Not a first-line treatment for an acute, severe episode; use it after the main symptoms have improved.
Focusing on well-being should never minimize real distress or adversity; validate first.
Medication changes, including tapering, must be managed by the prescriber.

This intervention does not assess or decide risk. If suicidal thoughts, self-harm or risk to others come up, pause and follow your setting's risk-assessment and safety-planning procedures. Keep crisis options visible: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US, call or text), the local emergency number, and findahelpline.com for other countries.
culturalAdaptations: Ideas of well-being differ: autonomy may matter less than harmony or family duty for some clients; adapt the dimensions to the client's values.
Use the client's own words for good moments and for what makes life meaningful.
Use a trained professional interpreter rather than family members, and check that key ideas carry the intended meaning in the client's language.
